title: Matthew 27:57–61
context: Evening falls. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new rock tomb; Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary sit opposite, watching.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 27:57–61.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: When the evening was come - That is, after three o'clock; the time from three to six they termed the evening.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 27:57–61)

reformed.quote: Let it be understood that Joseph did not come in the dusk of the evening, but before sunset, that he might perform this office of kindness to his Master, without violating the Sabbath; for the Sabbath commenced in the evening, and therefore it was necessary that Christ should be laid in the grave before night came on. Now from the time that Christ died until the Sabbath began to be observed, there were three free days.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 27:57–61)

verses.text: When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathaea named Joseph, who himself was also Jesus’ disciple, came.
verses.arminianNotes:
Evening brings Joseph—rich, named, a disciple. Courage surfaces when the body needs burying.

Grace can embolden hidden disciples at the needed hour. Wealth is no barrier when put to Christ’s honor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph of Arimathea steps forward. Providence supplies a tomb through a rich disciple.

God had prepared burial means. Isaiah’s “with a rich man in his death” hangs over the scene.

verses.text: This man went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Then Pilate commanded the body to be given up.
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks Pilate for the body—public identification with the Crucified. Pilate grants it.

Costly association is part of discipleship. Grace enables going public when fear would stay home.
verses.reformedNotes:
Body requested and given. Rome releases what it killed; God steers the corpse toward a known tomb.

No lost body, no anonymous pit. Providence guards the burial for Easter’s sake.

verses.text: Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth
verses.arminianNotes:
Clean linen for a holy body. Care replaces the morning’s scorn.

Love handles Jesus with honor. Grace teaches reverence for the Lord who died for us.
verses.reformedNotes:
Clean shroud: dignity in burial. The Passion’s humiliation does not end in refuse.

Even burial details serve the story God is telling toward resurrection.

verses.text: and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the door of the tomb, and departed.
verses.arminianNotes:
His own new tomb, rock-cut, stone rolled. Jesus rests in a borrowed, unused grave.

He occupies death’s space for us. Grace invites trust that the stone is not the last word.
verses.reformedNotes:
New tomb, great stone: secure by human measure. The stage is set for a sealed, guarded, then empty grave.

God appoints a known tomb so resurrection will be public, not private spiritualizing.

verses.text: Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary, sitting opposite the tomb.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two Marys sit opposite the tomb—watching, grieving, remembering the place.

The women’s faithful presence matters. Grace keeps witnesses near so hope can find them at dawn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Women opposite the tomb: continuity of witness from cross to burial.

They know the location. Easter morning will not be a hunt for the wrong grave.
